title: Advanced Safety Features

jokes.text: I've emailed every former student who's not in prison or jail. Everyone, remember, there's a difference. Our alumni are touchy about that.
jokes.setup: Frankie gives a routine administrative update about alumni outreach
jokes.punchline: The distinction between prison and jail implies enough alumni are incarcerated that the semantic difference matters — and they're 'touchy' about it
jokes.explanation: Frankie's deadpan delivery of institutional dysfunction is well-calibrated. The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of the distinction mattering, and the dark implication about Greendale's alumni. Character-specific because it's exactly the kind of precise bureaucratic pedantry Frankie would voice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: The difference is that prison is where you go after you're convicted of a crime. Jail is where you go when you're arrested and waiting for trial.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: But really, prison requires proving you're poor. Jail is just cop bias.

jokes.text: What's the difference? You go to jail if a cop doesn't like you. They can't send you to prison without knowing you're poor.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what the difference between prison and jail is
jokes.punchline: Britta gives an aggressively politicized non-answer that is both wrong and completely on-brand
jokes.explanation: Pure Britta — she answers a factual question with identity politics that isn't even coherent. The character integration is near-perfect; this joke couldn't come from anyone else. The follow-up 'Do you believe half your own politics?' from Jeff is implied and elevates it further.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm looking for a good DJ.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I don't understand what makes DJs different from basic technology.

jokes.text: Do you believe half your own politics? Yeah.
jokes.setup: Britta delivers a non-answer about prison vs. jail
jokes.punchline: Jeff's weary challenge, and Britta's honest, unashamed 'Yeah' — she only half-believes her own rhetoric
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words carry years of character history. 'Yeah.' from Britta is a gem: she's self-aware enough to admit she's performing, but not enough to stop. The exchange efficiently defines both Jeff (cynical, sharp) and Britta (authentic in her inauthenticity).

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'd like to begin my PowerPoint presentation.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I should tell you, I have no idea how to use PowerPoint.

jokes.text: I'm still trying to find a good deejay, by which I mean figure out what makes a deejay good. Or bad. Or different from a phone or laptop.
jokes.setup: Dean gives a progress report on the alumni dance deejay search
jokes.punchline: He reveals he doesn't understand what a deejay is at all — his 'by which I mean' construction is a confession of total ignorance
jokes.explanation: Good Dean moment — the escalating self-clarification that undercuts itself. The 'or different from a phone or laptop' kicker sells it. Competent character comedy, nothing exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I just know PowerPoint.

jokes.text: Chang's PowerPoint presentation — a Rube Goldberg sequence of charts, eggs, and a dollar bill that should have been a dollar bill but 'I'm no magician. I'm just a guy that knows PowerPoint.'
jokes.setup: Chang was asked how the PowerPoint is going; he said 'Yes' to knowing PowerPoint
jokes.punchline: His presentation is a bewildering series of non-sequitur slides culminating in him apparently trying to do a magic trick with an egg and a dollar bill, capped with sincere self-description as 'just a guy that knows PowerPoint'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sustained bits. The timestamps (00:44, 01:03, 01:13, 01:17, 01:22) show this is a slow-burn visual comedy sequence — the gaps between slides are the joke. 'That should have been a dollar bill. But I'm no magician. I'm just a guy that knows PowerPoint.' is a genuinely funny line because it's simultaneously self-aware and not self-aware. The character integration is excellent: Chang's self-delusion expressed through administrative incompetence.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need to try some guerrilla marketing.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Guerrilla? Like actual gorillas? That would be amazing!

jokes.text: Why do they need marketing? They're amazing.
jokes.setup: Dean warns about guerrilla marketing on campus
jokes.punchline: Britta hears 'guerrilla' and thinks of the animals, responding with earnest admiration
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta malapropism/mishearing. The wordplay is clean (guerrilla/gorilla), and the response 'They're amazing' is perfectly Britta — earnest, environmentally sympathetic, and completely wrong. Economy is excellent; four words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's like they're cleaning the glass of your mind with Windex.

jokes.text: Guerilla with a U. Got it.
jokes.setup: Dean corrects the guerilla/gorilla confusion
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'Got it' implies understanding but the correction is transparently meaningless to her — she's just moving on
jokes.explanation: Decent tag on the gorilla joke. 'Got it' implies total non-comprehension. Good economy but lighter than the original beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. A Honda Fit? THE Honda Fit?

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: I'm canceling school. Everything. All of it. Classes are canceled.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: We're all going to look at this car together as a community.

jokes.text: They can advertise things without you knowing? Is that legal? It sounds like brain windexing.
jokes.setup: Dean explains guerrilla marketing — covert advertising that blends into the public
jokes.punchline: 'Brain windexing' — a made-up term that is weirdly evocative and perfectly Abed in its clinical detachment
jokes.explanation: 'Brain windexing' is an exceptional coinage — it's precise, vivid, and strange. It captures the horror of subliminal advertising in two words. Only Abed would phrase it with this clinical neutrality ('Is that legal?' followed immediately by a consumer-products metaphor). One of the episode's best single lines. Highly quotable and original.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm going to have to freeze all of the school's assets.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: It's a freezy wheezy.

jokes.text: Someone just told me that Honda has released some kind of super vehicle called the Honda Fit. It's a small car with a big personality that can handle anything life throws at you. Why am I standing here talking about it? I have to find a Honda dealer, school is canceled. The Honda Fit! It's happening! It's finally happening! I'm just going to give the school's assets a quick freezie-weezie.
jokes.setup: Dean just finished warning everyone about guerrilla marketers — then immediately becomes a victim of one
jokes.punchline: Dean begins verbatim reciting Honda marketing copy in real-time, canceling school and announcing 'freezie-weezie' on the assets — entirely oblivious to the irony
jokes.explanation: Structurally masterful — the episode's central comic irony is established in one beat: the man who just warned the room about guerrilla marketing is immediately captured by it. 'It's happening! It's finally happening!' is perfect escalation. 'Freezie-weezie' is a great Dean-ism. The structure (setup: warning / punchline: immediate victimhood) is the kind of tight comedic architecture Community does best. High craft, high impact.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Is the meeting over?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Yes, Jeff, the meeting is over.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: So we can just... stay here and be funny?

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: That's basically what we do.

jokes.text: Is this meeting over? I think so, but sometimes we just hang out and say funny... stuff.
jokes.setup: The meeting has clearly dissolved into chaos after the Dean runs out
jokes.punchline: Jeff's pause before 'stuff' implies he was going to say something more colorful — plus the meta acknowledgment that the group just hangs out being 'funny'
jokes.explanation: Mildly meta — the show acknowledging its own premise. Jeff's self-censored 'stuff' is a decent beat but not exceptional. Elroy's straight-man question is functional setup.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: So let me get this straight. Jeff is the handsome one, Britta's the mess, Annie's the smart girl, Abed's the weird one, Troy's the lovable guy, and Shirley's... the mom?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pretty much.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Cool. So where do I fit in?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, you're the old guy.

jokes.text: Is he Black Pierce, Old Troy, or Shirley Without a Giant Purse?
jokes.setup: The group discusses whether Elroy likes them and what his 'role' in the group is
jokes.punchline: Jeff reduces all prior group members to reductive racial/age/accessory descriptors — making explicit the show's formula of archetype-slotting
jokes.explanation: Genuinely sharp meta-comedy. Jeff voicing the show's unspoken logic — that characters fill demographic slots — is both self-aware and funny in its callousness. 'Shirley Without a Giant Purse' is the funniest of the three because it reduces her defining trait to an accessory. High quotability. The joke works as character comedy (Jeff), meta-commentary, and tribute to departed characters simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: What was so special about Troy? Why won't anybody tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Was he a astronaut? Did he invent something? Was he bitten by a radioactive person?

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Did he teach you all how to love? Was he half-man, half-horse? A full horse that could talk?

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Could he do that thing where you move your finger really fast and it looks like there's two of them? Was he made of chocolate?

jokes.text: I haven't exactly been a whirlwind of entertainment since Troy left.
jokes.setup: Discussion of what Elroy's role in the group might be
jokes.punchline: Abed's self-assessment that he's been boring — delivered with his characteristic clinical flatness — is both sad and funny
jokes.explanation: Abed's self-awareness about his own diminished comedic energy post-Troy is a quietly effective character moment. The deadpan delivery makes it funnier than its content alone warrants.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: What made Troy so special?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He was really good at folding fitted sheets.

jokes.text: It's not just me. You guys have been boring, too.
jokes.setup: Group tries to reassure Abed that he's still entertaining
jokes.punchline: Abed accepts the compliment and immediately extends his self-criticism to everyone else
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed. He accepts the compliment ('That's not true. No, you're amazing.') and then immediately demolishes everyone else with the same logic. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy is an incredibly talented steel drum player. I'm telling you the truth right now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: See, in comedy, the setup and punchline need to have a clear relationship. You establish something in the setup, then subvert it in the punchline for maximum comedic effect.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So when I tell you Troy's steel drum skills are amazing, and then I explain the mechanics of how that joke should work, the irony is that I'm not actually giving you a punchline about Troy at all.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm just being completely honest about how this works.

jokes.text: What was so special about this Troy person? Did he own a rainbow? Was he the group's pharmacist?
jokes.setup: The group talks reverentially about Troy as if he were a mythic figure
jokes.punchline: Elroy's frustrated attempts to decode the reverence produce increasingly absurd guesses — 'did he own a rainbow' is surreal; 'was he the group's pharmacist' implies he was a drug dealer
jokes.explanation: Elroy as an outsider decoding Greendale mythology is a great comedic device this episode uses well. 'Did he own a rainbow' is a beautiful non-sequitur; 'the group's pharmacist' has an edge of dark implication. Elroy's pragmatic incredulity is a fresh perspective on a running meta-joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I don't... I genuinely don't remember how that trick was supposed to work.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Did I ever actually know? I think I just bought it from a magic shop and assumed I'd figure it out.

jokes.text: We don't like to talk about it. But you often do.
jokes.setup: Group says 'We don't like to talk about it' about Troy
jokes.punchline: Elroy immediately points out they talk about Troy constantly
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp — Elroy punctures the group's pretension in four words. The outsider-correcting-insider dynamic is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Your ex worked at Subway?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Don't say that name! Every time I hear it, I have a panic attack. That place ruined my life!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's just a sandwich shop, Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You owe me therapy money just for saying it out loud.

jokes.text: Troy was very gifted at steel drums.
jokes.setup: Elroy says he's a problem solver and asks for information about Troy
jokes.punchline: Abed distills Troy's entire character and the group's love for him into the most mundane, random possible fact
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. After building up Troy as a near-mythical figure, Abed's answer reduces him to a niche musical skill. The deadpan is crucial — Abed believes this IS the essential information. It's also a plant for the Elroy payoff (his steel drum interest). Character-specific, economical, structurally elegant.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been thinking about switching to a new phone. The new Samsung Galaxy has an amazing camera, incredible battery life, and the processing speed is just unbelievable. Plus, the 5G connectivity means I can stream anything instantly. It's really the phone for me.

jokes.text: Steel drums. Interesting. [long pause, Elroy leaves]
jokes.setup: Abed reveals Troy's steel drum gift as the key information
jokes.punchline: Elroy processes this, says 'Interesting' with clearly suppressed significance, then immediately excuses himself — the audience understands he plays steel drums before anyone else does
jokes.explanation: The rewatch bonus is high because on second viewing you realize Elroy is about to go practice steel drums. The pause and 'Interesting' are doing heavy lifting — it's a visual/reaction joke inferred from context. The planted callback structure is the episode's main B-plot engine.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: I'm Rick, but you might know me by my old nickname - The Sandwich Man.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Well, those days are behind me now. I'm declaring my independence. I'm Honda - the power of dreams.

jokes.text: That won't pay off immediately, but it's gonna pay off.
jokes.setup: Elroy has just left after hearing about Troy's steel drums, clearly connecting to something
jokes.punchline: Jeff narrates the sitcom's own structure — lampshading that this was a plant and predicting its payoff as if he's aware they're in a TV show
jokes.explanation: Jeff's meta-commentary on narrative structure is classic Community. It's both in-character (Jeff as the knowing cynic) and self-referential (the show acknowledging its own craft). Works better on rewatch when you know exactly how it pays off.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You need to crouch down so I can hit you properly. It's martial arts rules.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: What? That's not how this works.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Just crouch!

jokes.text: And that, Jeff, is the truth. [egg reveal — Chang is showing the dollar bill was inside the egg the whole time]
jokes.setup: Chang's earlier PowerPoint included an egg and an inexplicable dollar bill moment
jokes.punchline: Chang is apparently still running the trick — revealing the dollar bill was inside the egg — in the hallway after the meeting, as a callback to his PowerPoint disaster
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback. 'Did you lose the egg you put the dollar bill in? That's how it works?' from someone off-screen lands the punchline that Chang has continued his bizarre trick into the hallway. The structure of the callback rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Britta... I've missed you so much. I need to be real with you about something.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about what really matters in life, and it's moments like this. Connection. Authenticity. And that's why I want to tell you about the all-new Honda Civic with its spacious interior and exceptional fuel efficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: It gets 33 miles per gallon on the highway. I'm not just saying that—I really mean it.

jokes.text: Britta, remember that guy who you were in love with, but your love was torn asunder because he was the human incarnation of a certain sandwich franchise? Sub— Don't say it. Don't ever say that name without compensation.
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to warn Britta about something sensitive
jokes.punchline: The callback to Rick being the Subway brand spokesperson — and Britta's reflexive 'don't say that name without compensation' — implies she was traumatized enough to have brand-related PTSD with a legal/financial component
jokes.explanation: Good callback for returning viewers. 'Don't ever say that name without compensation' implies she's developed parasocial copyright instincts from her trauma — a quirky specific character detail. Works even without the prior episode context if you understand the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm doing guerrilla marketing for Honda.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: That's why it has to be secret. If people know it's an ad, it's not guerrilla marketing anymore—it's just regular marketing.

jokes.text: See, I don't just fling myself into the wild. The hub of a quality camping experience is a safe and reliable generator.
jokes.setup: Annie tells Britta not to run to Rick; Britta agrees she needs to be smarter; Annie says she'll meet her later
jokes.punchline: The moment Annie is gone, Britta is already walking toward Rick, delivering a Honda CR-V marketing line about 'generators' that she thinks is her own self-justifying wisdom
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — Britta's self-delusion and her susceptibility to marketing work together. The audience can tell she's already been influenced into walking toward Rick, and the 'generator' line foreshadows that Rick is marketing to her without her knowing. Ironic on multiple levels: she's the person who calls out corporate manipulation, and she's the most susceptible.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, we can just be friends.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Hey, as a friend, you gotta see this — check out the heated seats. Feel that? That's friendship right there.

jokes.text: Su— No, no, no, no. That's my sandwich name. I'm my own man, now. I'm a free, reliable, quality man... named Rick.
jokes.setup: Britta almost says 'Subway' (Rick's former corporate identity)
jokes.punchline: Rick corrects her — 'Subway' is his 'sandwich name' — and replaces it with language that is transparently Honda marketing copy ('reliable, quality') while claiming freedom
jokes.explanation: Smart joke — Rick claims independence from corporate identity while using Honda buzzwords ('reliable, quality') to describe himself. The irony is subtle enough that Britta doesn't catch it, and the audience may not fully catch it on first viewing, making it a rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We should play something that really shows Elroy how fun we are.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What about Cards Against Humanity?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's literally just us trying to seem edgy and cool in front of the new guy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Perfect. Let's play 'Cards Against Humanity: Please Like Us, Elroy.'

jokes.text: That's for half of my heart. And that's for the other half. And this is for being the reason there's two halves of my heart.
jokes.setup: Britta and Rick reunite; she's been learning karate (yellow belt)
jokes.punchline: Britta delivers three increasingly portentous punches/kicks to Rick with emotional narration — the escalation of 'two halves of my heart' is simultaneously earnest and absurd
jokes.explanation: Decent physical/verbal escalation. The logic of 'and this is for being the reason there's two halves' is delightfully circular. Britta's earnest melodrama is in character. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We chose this game for you because we thought it really matched your personality.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What game is it?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Candyland.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Candyland? Why would you—

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Because your life peaked in the '80s and now you're just trying to recapture that magic by visiting imaginary places.

jokes.text: Can you actually crouch down a little bit 'cause you're taller than my instructor and I'm only a yellow belt.
jokes.setup: Britta is delivering emotionally charged karate strikes to Rick during their reunion
jokes.punchline: Mid-emotional-climax, Britta breaks to make a practical request about technique limitations — undercutting her own drama with mundane logistics
jokes.explanation: Excellent deflation joke. The sudden pivot from emotional karate to practical logistics ('I'm only a yellow belt') is perfectly timed. It encapsulates Britta's character: she's trying to be badass and romantic but is fundamentally limited and self-aware about it. The 'my instructor' detail makes it funnier — she's comparing Rick to her actual karate teacher.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not old enough to play this game.

jokes.text: The windows are fogged over. Are you napping heavily? I can't hide forever. No, but you can hide in comfort. There's 35.2 cubic feet of cargo space back here.
jokes.setup: Rick and Britta are having a romantic moment in the Honda CR-V; Dean arrives
jokes.punchline: Rick hides from Dean in the cargo area and Britta helps sell him on it using actual Honda specs — 'you can hide in comfort, 35.2 cubic feet' — turning a desperate practical problem into a sales pitch
jokes.explanation: Good sustained irony — the Honda cargo space spec delivered as romantic reassurance is funny because Britta is both sincerely trying to help and unconsciously doing Honda's marketing work. 'Are you napping heavily?' is a funny line in its own right.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: You know, in a space this compact, most people would feel claustrophobic. But look at these dimensions - 6 feet by 4 feet of pure cargo comfort. That's 24 square feet of intimate potential.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Rick, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, the Honda Civic has won 'Best Compact Interior' for three years running. The headroom alone - a full 37 inches - allows for any position you might want to... explore.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: And the climate control system means you'll never get too hot. Well, unless you want to. Which, statistically, 60% of compact car owners report preferring.

jokes.text: Why choose when you can Hond-oose?
jokes.setup: Dean has bought both a Honda Fit and a CR-V
jokes.punchline: 'Hond-oose' — a portmanteau of Honda and 'choose' — is exactly the kind of ad slogan a Level Seven Susceptible would invent for himself
jokes.explanation: Dean Pelton creating his own Honda portmanteau slogan is perfectly in character. The word is immediately comprehensible and funny. High character integration — this is exactly what an enthusiastic, unrestrained super-consumer would do.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know what they say... when it comes to Honda, you really gotta... *Honda* choose!

jokes.text: Oh, and that blower. That was just an impulse buy.
jokes.setup: Dean reveals he bought two Hondas
jokes.punchline: He also bought a blower — a third Honda product, presented as the most casual afterthought
jokes.explanation: Decent escalation beat. The 'impulse buy' framing for a Honda power blower is funny. Relies on the Dean's established excess rather than fresh comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Look at this Honda Civic. Isn't she beautiful?

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Dean, you've been saying that about every Honda for the past hour.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Because they ARE beautiful!

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to classify you as a Level 5 Marketing Susceptibility case. You're the most vulnerable to advertising I've ever seen.

jokes.text: My God. You're a Level Seven Susceptible.
jokes.setup: Dean has bought two Hondas and a blower after one conversation with Rick
jokes.punchline: Britta identifies a specific categorization — 'Level Seven Susceptible' — as if it's a known, formal scale, delivered with the gravity of a medical diagnosis
jokes.explanation: The term 'Level Seven Susceptible' is a great coinage — it sounds like it's from an official document or a D&D stat sheet. The specificity of 'seven' (not five, not ten) makes it funnier. It becomes a running gag through the episode and pays off at the end when Britta admits she's one too.

jokes.text: A what? Uh, nothing. Nothing, I... Look, Rick. Whatever that is, you can tell me. I'm on board. Yes. Hmm. Yes, you are.
jokes.setup: Britta identifies the Dean as a Level Seven Susceptible and tries to walk it back
jokes.punchline: Rick immediately accepts the concept, and the word 'susceptible' applies to him assessing Britta — 'Yes, you are' — implying Britta herself is being recruited
jokes.explanation: Rick's 'Yes, you are' — referring to Britta being susceptible to him — is a smooth, slightly sinister turn. It reframes the Level Seven concept as applying to Britta and Rick's relationship, adding a layer. Good structural use of the concept.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Elroy, we'd like to thank you for flying Community. We know you had choices, and we're grateful you chose to spend your layover with us.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We hope you enjoyed your time at our gate. Should you decide to return, we'll be here, same time next week.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Until then, we wish you clear skies and tailwinds, my friend.

jokes.text: Am I found in Africa? Yes and San Diego and the Bronx. A woman? Am I large? Am I an elephant? I was thinking dolphin but I knew they didn't have ears because my dentist has a poster of one on the ceiling and I recently had a root canal.
jokes.setup: The group plays 'The Ears Have It' — a game about identifying whose ears you have
jokes.punchline: Chang's reasoning for his elephant guess includes a completely non-sequitur dentist anecdote — 'my dentist has a dolphin poster and I recently had a root canal' — delivered as if it's perfectly logical
jokes.explanation: The dentist non-sequitur is the gem here — Chang's associative logic is funny because it's internally coherent in a broken way. The root canal detail is a perfect absurdist touch. The game itself is a good backdrop for character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're right. That pun... it wasn't just funny. It was actually saying something about how I'm always trying to be the responsible one, keeping everyone in line.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Elroy just called me out without even really calling me out.

jokes.text: Hey, party people. I could hear you all the way down the hall. We're playing The Ears Have It. Chang's ahead by three pair. With an asterisk. I'm cheating.
jokes.setup: Elroy arrives and the group reports Chang's score
jokes.punchline: Chang immediately and cheerfully volunteers that he's cheating — with zero shame
jokes.explanation: Chang's cheerful self-incrimination is well-deployed. 'With an asterisk. I'm cheating.' has great rhythm — the asterisk qualification is funnier than a straight confession would be.

dialogue.speaker: Shane
dialogue.line: I cheat at everything. Cards, board games, sports, you name it.

dialogue.speaker: Shane
dialogue.line: Actually, right now I'm cheating at a completely different game somewhere else.

jokes.text: Well, fun hanging out with you, Elroy. We know you have your choice of friends and we thank you for choosing us.
jokes.setup: Elroy arrives and there's a chaotic crash (Whoa!/Oh no!)
jokes.punchline: Jeff's airline-announcement-style farewell — 'we know you have your choice of friends and we thank you for choosing us' — is transparently insincere corporate-speak used to dismiss someone
jokes.explanation: Jeff's airline-service phrasing is a sharp register collision — the forced warmth of customer service language applied to social interaction. Very Jeff: polished surface concealing indifference. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Oh! Ow! Son of a— What the— Are you kidding me?! I swear to— Oh for crying out— Why does this always— WHAT IS WRONG WITH THIS—

jokes.text: I got up to make nachos, and Elroy said that was 'not-cho' job, and we laughed. Then he made them for me. It was more than wordplay. It really wasn't my job in his eyes.
jokes.setup: Annie explains what happened at the game night to make Elroy warm up
jokes.punchline: The 'not-cho' pun is the stated joke, but Annie's sincere deconstruction of it — 'it was more than wordplay' — is the actual comedy. She over-interprets a nacho pun as a profound moment of connection.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The 'not-cho' pun is deliberately weak — but Annie's sincere earnest over-analysis ('it was more than wordplay. It really wasn't my job in his eyes.') transforms it into a character joke about Annie's desperate need for connection and meaning. The layers: weak pun + Annie's sincerity + the fact that she's right that it meant something to Elroy = genuinely funny and touching.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: You should try this scotch. It's smooth, complex, really exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: What makes it so special?

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Well, the label has a really nice thistle on it.

jokes.text: It's not true, you know? Oh, it is. I cheat my ass off at everything. I'm cheating at a game of hide and seek right now. We weren't supposed to leave the rec center.
jokes.setup: Someone disputes Chang's asterisk/cheating claim
jokes.punchline: Chang escalates from cheating at The Ears Have It to confessing he is currently cheating at a completely different, ongoing game of hide and seek — which he has broken the rules of by leaving the rec center
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The escalation from cheating at a card game to 'I'm cheating at hide and seek right now' is a perfect surprise — it implies Chang's entire life involves parallel games he's cheating at simultaneously. 'We weren't supposed to leave the rec center' is a devastating kicker that specifies the cheating with bureaucratic precision. High originality, structure, character integration, and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Honda Representative
dialogue.line: What about billboards and commercials?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, billboards are just lies on a stick, and commercials are like... commie-ercials, because they're trying to control us with propaganda.

jokes.text: Rick's Honda boss ('Hilary') as a bartender, steering Britta toward an expensive scotch through authentic-seeming expertise
jokes.setup: Britta goes to a bar for a club soda; a friendly bartender guides her toward premium scotch
jokes.punchline: The 'helpful' bartender is later revealed to be Rick's Honda boss, staging a demonstration of covert marketing on Britta — the entire warm interaction was manufactured
jokes.explanation: The scene is funnier in retrospect. On first view it's a pleasant bar interaction; on rewatch every word is a sales technique. The structure of using cringe-retroactive comedy (the discomfort comes when you realize you've been watching a manipulation) is well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Honda Rep
dialogue.line: We prefer to think of it as... a gentle awakening of consumer desire. Like a soft massage for the mind.

dialogue.speaker: Honda Rep
dialogue.line: We're not manipulating you. We're simply creating a serene environment where your needs and our products harmoniously align.

dialogue.speaker: Honda Rep
dialogue.line: It's all very spa-like. Very therapeutic. You'll leave feeling relaxed and wanting to finance a Honda Civic.

jokes.text: It's got a pig on the bottle. But this one, this one's really good. It's aged eight years, smoky, from Scotland. A little pricier but worth it. I drink this one when I've got a reason to celebrate.
jokes.setup: The Honda boss asks what scotch Britta recommends
jokes.punchline: Britta goes into full enthusiastic connoisseur mode, recommending the expensive one — but this is a setup for her being manipulated into celebrating with the boss's preferred scotch
jokes.explanation: Modest setup beat. Britta's bartender expertise being weaponized against her is thematically resonant but not especially funny in isolation. Gets better on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, I was manipulated into buying this? I thought I chose it because it was sophisticated.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's what marketing is, Britta. They're very good at making you think you want things.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: But if they can make me want scotch I don't need, what else are they making me want?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Everything. Your clothes, your music, your sense of humor.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Who am I even?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And if they can control your wants, can they control your feelings?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Do I even love anyone, or was that marketing too?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, that escalated quickly.

jokes.text: Do you enjoy billboards and commercials, Miss Perry? You mean shill-boards and con-mercials?
jokes.setup: Hilary pitches guerrilla marketing as preferable to traditional advertising
jokes.punchline: Britta's immediate rebranding — 'shill-boards and con-mercials' — is her reflex anticorporate wordplay
jokes.explanation: 'Shill-boards and con-mercials' is a great Britta coinage — it's the kind of portmanteau a person with her politics would spontaneously generate. Character-specific wordplay at its best. 'Con-mercials' especially works because 'con' has a double meaning (con artist + abbreviation of commercial).

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm being obnoxious. My girlfriend just left me because I spent all our money on a Honda CR-V, and I've been acting out. I apologize.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: But seriously, have you seen the cargo space on that thing? It's ridiculous. I mean, my girlfriend's gone, but at least I can fit a whole deer in there if I wanted to.

jokes.text: He finds that part of each life that Honda can improve and gently bathes it in the most helpful information possible. I don't think you understand how surgery works.
jokes.setup: Hilary describes Rick's guerrilla marketing as 'surgical' — finding the right spot and applying information
jokes.punchline: Britta calls out that the surgery metaphor doesn't work — 'I don't think you understand how surgery works' — a correct logical point delivered as a withering deflation
jokes.explanation: Good logical deflation joke. Britta's critique is actually correct — 'bathing in information' is not surgery — and the mundane accuracy of her rebuttal is what makes it funny. Works as both a character moment (Britta refusing to be charmed) and a straight joke.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: So Rick is really special to you, huh? I mean, you've really got him pegged.

dialogue.speaker: Todd
dialogue.line: You know, pegged. Like you really understand him. You've got him pegged.

jokes.text: I came in here to get a club soda. Right now I am drinking probably the best scotch I've had in years. Did you trick me? Am I suffering?
jokes.setup: Britta realizes she's been manipulated into drinking expensive scotch
jokes.punchline: 'Am I suffering?' — Britta's indignant anti-corporate stance collides with the fact that the manipulation improved her evening; she can't even claim victimhood convincingly
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'Am I suffering?' is the core thesis of the whole Honda satire — guerrilla marketing that actually delivers something you enjoy undermines the moral outrage. Britta being unable to maintain her victimhood because the scotch is good is both funny and philosophically coherent. High character integration, structure, and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Stay away from the mechanic.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Unless you're using a candy tool.

jokes.text: Do you love this man? I do. Then I pronounce you a highly influential couple. You may kiss your boyfriend.
jokes.setup: Hilary pitches Britta on becoming a marketing couple with Rick
jokes.punchline: Hilary performs a mock wedding ceremony to seal the deal — 'I pronounce you a highly influential couple' — framing a corporate partnership as a romantic union
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist moment — Hilary's corporate authority expressed through wedding ceremony language is funny. 'Highly influential couple' as a marriage vow is a nice bit. The 'where'd he go?' reaction that follows is a good tag.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm like a human skunk. Not because I'm clever or resourceful, but because I spray a noxious odor that makes people want to avoid me at all costs.

jokes.text: Wait, where'd he go? Well, that's not for us to understand. [pause] Well, okay, but he's right there.
jokes.setup: Rick seems to have disappeared dramatically after the 'ceremony'
jokes.punchline: Hilary delivers a mystical non-answer ('That's not for us to understand') but Rick is immediately visible — deflating the mystique instantly
jokes.explanation: Good deflation beat. Hilary's mystical non-answer is punctured by the mundane reality that Rick is just standing nearby. The gap between the posed mystique and banal reality is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so the band is called... Natalie's Freezing?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No wait, Natalie's Freezing?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Natalie's Freezing!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: NATALIE'S FREEZING?!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: NATALIE'S FREEZING!!!

jokes.text: I love antiquing. Everything is so old.
jokes.setup: Rick says he's excited about going antiquing with Britta; Britta says she loves it too
jokes.punchline: Britta's explanation of why she loves antiquing — 'everything is so old' — is a tautology delivered with sincerity
jokes.explanation: Britta's circular non-explanation is a small gem. It's the kind of thing a person says when they want to seem cultured but haven't thought it through. Perfect economy — four words, complete character encapsulation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why wouldn't he just admit it?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Because that's crazy person nonsense.

jokes.text: I hated finding these treasures and not being able to fit them in the car. Now I got a CR-V.
jokes.setup: Rick says he previously said he hated antiquing
jokes.punchline: His explanation for the change — he used to hate it because of storage limitations — is transparently a Honda cargo space sales pitch delivered as a personal epiphany
jokes.explanation: Good beat in the sustained Honda satire. Rick's life narrative seamlessly integrated with product specs is the episode's central comic mechanism working well.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I have a rule about being constructive.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: All my questions would just be insults disguised as questions.

jokes.text: It's kind of a game-changer. It's certainly a sex-life changer. Sorry.
jokes.setup: Todd says the CR-V is 'kind of a game-changer'
jokes.punchline: Britta escalates 'game-changer' to 'sex-life changer' — oversharing in public — then immediately apologizes, suggesting she both means it and knows it's too much
jokes.explanation: Good Britta beat — her overshare followed by 'sorry' is well-timed. Also works as a Honda joke: they've now had sex in the CR-V cargo space (referencing the fogged windows scene). The economy of the pivot from Todd's comment to 'sex-life changer' is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: These Honda floor mats are really top quality.

dialogue.speaker: Britta's Mom
dialogue.line: You know, I never really thought about floor mats before, but now I'm wondering if ours are even adequate.

jokes.text: You're amazing. You're amazing. Honda's amazing. I want you to meet my parents. Yes. Honda...
jokes.setup: Britta and Rick are deep in romantic rapport
jokes.punchline: Their declarations of love to each other keep sliding into Honda appreciation — the corporation has become a third party in the relationship
jokes.explanation: Good sustained irony — the relationship and the brand have merged completely. 'Honda's amazing' landing in the middle of personal declarations of love is the satire made explicit. Solid but relies on accumulated context.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, so your parents want to watch Avatar? That's great, because nothing says 'quality family time' like three hours of blue cat people having sex in a forest while corporations destroy the environment. It's basically a documentary about my parents' retirement portfolio.

jokes.text: Look, Britta's in love. Yep. He must be a very special young man. I bet they'll be together for a very long time. You got her pegged, man. Pegged.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Elroy watch Britta being clearly blissful with Rick
jokes.punchline: Elroy's sincere romantic optimism is punctured by Jeff's knowing 'Pegged' — which could mean Elroy has correctly assessed Britta's pattern, or the opposite; Jeff's 'Pegged' is loaded with irony given what we know about Britta and Rick
jokes.explanation: Jeff's ironic 'Pegged' is good but relatively subtle — the joke depends on the viewer reading Jeff's cynicism correctly. Decent character-specific moment.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: You booked my ex's band? Man, you're like a mannequin. You got the same blank stare, the same dead eyes, the same complete inability to understand how your actions affect real people. You're not even a person, Jeff. You're just a plastic shell that wanders around making everybody's life worse.

jokes.text: Hey, stay away from that mechanic. Unless I need a wrench made of licorice.
jokes.setup: Jeff gives Elroy a list of Natalie is Freezing charity album songs; Elroy seems charmed but says something dismissive to Jeff
jokes.punchline: 'Unless I need a wrench made of licorice' — a completely unexpected qualifier that implies Elroy has specific, bizarre needs that only a mechanic could meet, delivered as if 'wrench made of licorice' is a normal concept
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best single lines. 'A wrench made of licorice' is a surreal image that is completely specific and inexplicable — what scenario requires a licorice wrench? The confidence with which Elroy delivers it as a reasonable exception makes it funnier. High originality and quotability. Classic Community absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Are you Natalie from 'Natalie is Freezing'?

dialogue.speaker: Julie
dialogue.line: I'm an artist. I don't do commercial work.

jokes.text: Oh, I'm... I'm sorry. Inside joke.
jokes.setup: Elroy says the licorice wrench line and realizes he needs to explain himself to Jeff
jokes.punchline: He calls it an 'inside joke' — but the joke was between him and himself, not with Jeff; it was just a private absurdist thought
jokes.explanation: Decent tag. 'Inside joke' as an explanation for a solo absurdist thought is mildly funny but doesn't add much beyond the original line.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: I've devoted my life to Honda marketing. It's not just a job, it's a calling. I feel the hand of God pushing me towards those sales figures.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: When I close a deal, I hear the music from Chariots of Fire in my head. I'm running towards that finish line, and Honda is right there beside me.

jokes.text: Man, I'm like a fart to that guy. He can't get away fast enough. What? No. I mean, maybe.
jokes.setup: Jeff watches Elroy leave quickly after the interaction
jokes.punchline: 'I'm like a fart to that guy' — an unexpectedly crude self-comparison from usually image-conscious Jeff; Annie's 'No. I mean, maybe.' is the honest honesty he doesn't want
jokes.explanation: The 'fart' simile from Jeff is funny because it's undignified for him. Annie's 'No. I mean, maybe.' is a perfect beat — the honesty of 'maybe' is exactly the cruelty and care Annie brings simultaneously. Great character pairing.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: It's like when you have that thing that goes up and down to let people cross over the moat, you know what I'm talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: What is that called?

jokes.text: Oh, I'm sure you have detailed files on human vulnerability, Abed. What... oh!
jokes.setup: Abed suggests Jeff needs to show vulnerability to connect with Elroy
jokes.punchline: Jeff's sarcastic dismissal of Abed ('you have detailed files on human vulnerability') causes Abed to actually confirm it somehow — the 'What... oh!' suggests Abed produces evidence or reacts in a way that confirms the joke
jokes.explanation: Jeff's accusation landing as accurate (Abed likely does have such files) is a good character-based punchline. The 'What... oh!' reaction suggests physical comedy or a prop reveal that lands better visually.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: It's a bridge, but it goes up and down.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: A see-saw bridge?

jokes.text: Natalie is Freezing. Ugh. Natalie is Freezing. Natalie is Freezing. Natalie is Freezing... Natalie is Freezing. Natalie is Freezing. Natalie is Freezing...
jokes.setup: Jeff mispronounces 'Natalie is Freezing' as 'Natasha Freezes'
jokes.punchline: The group forces Jeff to repeat the correct band name multiple times as a correction ritual — the repetition becomes a comedic incantation
jokes.explanation: The repetition works through sheer escalation — the group's insistence on the correction becomes funnier the more times it repeats. Sets up the band name payoff when the actual band appears.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Yes! Yes, that's it! Drawbridge! Drawbridge, drawbridge, drawbridge!

jokes.text: What is this? I don't know. I... I don't know. Honda. The power of dreams.
jokes.setup: Rick does something to Britta — possibly an intimate gesture, or shows her something — and she can't articulate how she feels
jokes.punchline: He explains it with the actual Honda tagline — 'The power of dreams' — delivered as a sincere explanation for their connection
jokes.explanation: The Honda tagline delivered as a sincere explanation for a romantic moment is the episode's central satire at its most compressed. 'The power of dreams' as a straight answer to 'what is this?' is funny because it works emotionally even as it's transparently a corporate slogan.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. One last job. What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: We need you to test drive the new Honda Civic and give your honest opinion.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: My honest opinion? It's the most beautiful car I've ever seen. The way the light hits the hood is like poetry. I've never felt so alive behind the wheel. Honda really understands the human soul.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait... oh no. Oh no no no. I did it again, didn't I?

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: You really are susceptible to marketing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm a psychology major! I should be immune to this! But here I am, falling for it every single time.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton, I know how susceptible you are to advertising. Would you say I'm a Level Seven Susceptible? No. Because why would I? Because that's moon man talk.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts the Dean about being manipulated by Honda guerrilla marketing
jokes.punchline: The Dean dismisses 'Level Seven Susceptible' as 'moon man talk' — an expression that perfectly captures his defensive obliviousness
jokes.explanation: 'Moon man talk' is a great Deanism — vague, dismissive, and slightly nonsensical in exactly the way Dean Pelton would express skepticism. Good callback to the Level Seven concept.

dialogue.speaker: Julie
dialogue.line: Fine.

dialogue.speaker: Julie
dialogue.line: That was me doing an impression of you.

dialogue.speaker: Julie
dialogue.line: You're a jerk.

jokes.text: Are you... I don't know how to... I have a rule about being constructive, so I can't ask any questions right now because all the questions that I have right now are rhetorical and they end with the word idiot.
jokes.setup: Britta defends Rick using her circular logic about prior corporate espionage
jokes.punchline: Frankie's self-imposed 'constructive questions only' rule means she physically cannot respond to Britta's idiocy without breaking her own code — the restraint IS the joke
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Frankie's self-imposed rule creates a perfect comic trap — her competence and restraint collide with her obvious desire to call Britta an idiot. 'They all end with the word idiot' is a great line. 'Do you know what a rhetorical... no, of course you don't know what that is, you're an idiot... I'm sorry' is a perfect breakdown of her composure. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: I had nothing to do with this. This was all them.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: But since you're here, let me tell you about Hawthorne Wipes. Sixty percent more surface area. Three-ply. Hypoallergenic. Biodegradable. And they come in three designer colors: taupe, eggshell, and cream. We've won numerous awards.

jokes.text: I am so sorry, but you're so stupid. You have no idea, and you're the only one who has no idea, because guess why. Don't answer that. You'll get it wrong. Aw, so dumb. You're just a dumb little man who tries to destroy this school every minute... I am sorry! I'm so sorry.
jokes.setup: Frankie tries to maintain composure after Britta's backwards logic
jokes.punchline: Frankie completely loses her composure in a sustained, escalating tirade — 'Don't answer that. You'll get it wrong.' is a devastating mid-rant instruction — before catching herself and apologizing repeatedly
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Frankie's composure-maintenance setup. 'Don't answer that. You'll get it wrong.' is a highlight — it preemptively blocks any defense, adding insult to insult. 'Dumb little man' is a funny specific diminutive. The oscillation between tirade and 'I'm sorry' is a great character breakdown. This and joke 58 together form one of the episode's best sustained sequences.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown child
dialogue.line: No, you're playing it wrong. You're supposed to say 'ears have it' and then give an instruction that's impossible to do.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown child
dialogue.line: Like... okay, everybody change ears.

jokes.text: Oh! Oh, it's okay. I mean it's not okay, but... shh. Shh, shh, shh, shh. Oh, so stupid. Oh, shh, shh, shh. Such a dummy.
jokes.setup: Frankie has completely broken down and is simultaneously apologizing to and insulting Britta
jokes.punchline: She alternates between comforting 'shh shh shh' and insulting 'such a dummy' in the same breath — she physically can't stop herself
jokes.explanation: The 'shh shh / such a dummy' alternation is a genuinely funny physical comedy bit — Frankie both consoling and insulting simultaneously. This is a great showcase for the character: her control breaking down but her instinct to be kind fighting with her intelligence's revulsion. The rhythm of the alternation matters.

dialogue.speaker: Britta's Dad
dialogue.line: How did you know I was an elephant?

dialogue.speaker: Britta's Mom
dialogue.line: Because you're not an animal, you're just fat.

jokes.text: We are just so thrilled that you brought a friend. Thrilled. And it is 'friend,' then? I mean, is that the correct moniker? Boyfriend. This is... well that's... whoa!
jokes.setup: Britta brings Rick to meet her parents for the first time
jokes.punchline: Her mother's excessive 'Thrilled. THRILLED.' performance betrays something other than thrilled — the moniker investigation ('is that the correct moniker?') and then the melodramatic 'whoa!' at 'boyfriend' suggest this is a rare event
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe comedy — the parents' exaggerated reaction to something ordinary (a boyfriend) is a good implied joke about Britta's romantic history. 'Whoa!' at the word 'boyfriend' is effective.

jokes.text: Boy, you could just bowl me over with one of those, um, uh... sweetheart, you know, what are the, uh... you remember at the Johnson's cabin... Feathers. You could bowl me over with a feather.
jokes.setup: George is so surprised he can't complete his idiom
jokes.punchline: He needs his wife to supply the word 'feathers' — his surprise has caused a complete vocabulary failure — and the callback to 'the Johnson's cabin' implies they've discussed idioms there before
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — George's idiom failure is a funny specific detail. The 'Johnson's cabin' as a reference point for the word 'feather' is a surreal specificity that elevates an otherwise standard confused-dad bit.

jokes.text: It reminds me of the quality floor mats in my Honda CR-V. Oh, come on, sweetie, that's not necessary. You refer to your floor mats as 'quality.' I've never heard that level of floor-mat enthusiasm.
jokes.setup: Rick compliments the carpet at Britta's parents' house
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to Honda floor mats — 'quality floor mats' — even in a family-meeting context; Deb's sincere 'I've never heard that level of floor-mat enthusiasm' shows the manipulation landing on a new target
jokes.explanation: Good Honda satire continued into the family visit. Deb's earnest observation — 'I've never heard that level of floor-mat enthusiasm' — is funny because she's right and it doesn't make her suspicious. The parents as new susceptibles is a good extension of the episode's theme.

jokes.text: Should we be caring more about our floor mats, George? I don't think we need to jump to conclusions, Deb. Just let the man finish his story. They're floor mats, that's the story.
jokes.setup: Deb asks George if they're neglecting their floor mats after Rick's enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: George's patient 'just let the man finish his story' and Britta's flat 'They're floor mats, that's the story' are a perfect sequence — George is already half-susceptible while Britta tries to prevent the marketing from landing
jokes.explanation: 'They're floor mats, that's the story.' is a great line — Britta's frustrated reductionism puncturing the story George wants to hear. The parents as a microcosm of the episode's manipulation dynamics is well-deployed. George's patient open-mindedness vs. Britta's angry realism is a good comic contrast.

jokes.text: Hey, what's this? What's that? Look all around. There's things all around us. Would you like to see a movie? We have one. What is it, George? It's, uh, it's the, uh... The Aviator! N-no... The Avatar. Uh, no, thank you. That movie is three hours of puke.
jokes.setup: George awkwardly tries to redirect the conversation from floor mats
jokes.punchline: He can't remember the movie title (confusing Aviator and Avatar), and Britta's immediate 'three hours of puke' is a visceral, unfiltered dismissal
jokes.explanation: 'Three hours of puke' is a quotable line — specific, visceral, unequivocal. George's Aviator/Avatar confusion is a good character bit. The two jokes layer well: George's bumbling and Britta's unfiltered contempt for Avatar.

jokes.text: Of course, Britta's joking. We enjoy Avatar very much. We do? Yes. It's an immensely popular movie. Of course, we love it.
jokes.setup: Britta says Avatar is 'three hours of puke' in front of her parents
jokes.punchline: Rick immediately overrides Britta's opinion with one that's more market-friendly — 'it's an immensely popular movie' — correcting her authentic view with the consensus opinion required for guerrilla marketing
jokes.explanation: The Avatar joke is excellent as a vehicle for the episode's satire. Rick substituting 'immensely popular' for 'good' — popularity as the operative value judgment in marketing — is a sharp observation delivered as comedy. 'Of course, we love it' as a command is slightly chilling and very funny.

jokes.text: You're not gonna need a deejay. I've been saying that since the invention of the shuffle button.
jokes.setup: Discussion of the alumni dance deejay situation
jokes.punchline: Elroy's anti-deejay stance is so old it dates back to the shuffle button's invention — implying he's been having this argument for decades
jokes.explanation: Good character-building moment for Elroy — the shuffle button reference dates his perspective and implies a long-held contrarian opinion. Decent observational comedy, nothing exceptional.

jokes.text: Are you out of your damn mind? What? You know this band? You know damn well I do. Why do you always... what... what, are you trying to get me to like you? No. Good. 'Cause it ain't working. You weird hair-gelled CPR dummy.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals he's booked Natalie is Freezing for the dance — Elroy's favorite band
jokes.punchline: 'You weird hair-gelled CPR dummy' — Elroy's insult lands perfectly; it captures Jeff's artificial good looks (CPR dummy) and his grooming (hair-gelled) in a memorably specific compound image
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the most quotable in the transcript. 'Hair-gelled CPR dummy' is a perfect insult — it nails Jeff Winger's appearance (lifeless plastic perfection, artificial charm, the grooming) in a way that feels completely fresh. It could only be said about Jeff. The setup (Jeff obviously trying to get Elroy to like him by booking the band, then claiming 'No') and Elroy's response ('Good. 'Cause it ain't working.') followed by the insult is a well-constructed three-beat sequence.

jokes.text: It's pomade! Ah.
jokes.setup: Elroy calls Jeff 'hair-gelled'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's only defense is a grooming pedantry correction — it's pomade, not hair gel — which both proves Elroy's point about Jeff's vanity and is immediately defeated by Elroy's dismissive 'Ah'
jokes.explanation: Perfect tag. Jeff defending himself against an insult by correcting only the grooming-product terminology — not denying the CPR dummy part — is one of the episode's funniest moments. It's completely in character (Jeff cares more about appearing sophisticated than about the actual insult) and the specificity (pomade vs. gel) is pitch-perfect vanity. 'Ah' from Elroy completing the exchange with total dismissal is the ideal button.

jokes.text: As long as I'm up here, does anyone want anything reached?
jokes.setup: Jeff is standing on a step stool or elevated position after the exchange
jokes.punchline: Jeff's attempt to salvage dignity after the dressing-down by offering a practical service — 'does anyone want anything reached?' — is pathetically gracious
jokes.explanation: Jeff's pivot to offering a mundane service (reaching things) after being destroyed is a great deflation beat. The offer itself is both a non-sequitur and deeply in character — Jeff turning his height into a utility in a moment of embarrassment. Gets called back later ('I've been practicing').

jokes.text: Hey. We're Natalie is Freezing. Oh, are you Natalie? I'm Julie. The name of the band is Natalie is Freezing. Why would anyone in the band be Natalie? We're artists. Cool.
jokes.setup: Natalie is Freezing arrives to perform; Dean greets them
jokes.punchline: Dean asks if she's Natalie — the obvious question — and Julie's indignant 'Why would anyone in the band be Natalie? We're artists.' is the perfect payoff for the episode-long band name repetition drill
jokes.explanation: One of the best payoffs in the episode. The entire episode has been building anticipation about this band's name, and when they finally arrive, Dean asks the obvious question everyone was thinking. Julie's indignant defense — 'We're artists' — is both the punchline and a perfect satire of indie band pretension. The structure (long setup of name correction ritual → first meeting reveals the irrationality was always there) is very well-crafted. High quotability.

jokes.text: So, our deejay was gonna man the frozen yogurt machine. Is that something that you guys can handle? If you do need anything reached, I've been practicing.
jokes.setup: Dean tries to recruit the band to also operate the yogurt machine
jokes.punchline: Jeff's callback to his 'anything reached?' offer — now claiming he's been 'practicing' reaching things in the interim — is a perfect button on a small running gag
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'I've been practicing' implies he went off and literally practiced reaching things in the time since his offer — a ridiculous commitment to a useless skill offered in a moment of embarrassment. Good callback structure.

jokes.text: We like Avatar? In public, yes, we like things most people like. Our job isn't to alienate people. We're on the job with my parents?
jokes.setup: Britta confronts Rick about pretending to like Avatar
jokes.punchline: Rick confirms they're always on the job — with everyone, everywhere, all the time — and Britta's horror that this extends to her parents is the revelation that their relationship has no private sphere
jokes.explanation: Good thematic beat that's also funny. 'We like things most people like' as a guiding philosophy is a sharp satire of marketing's relationship with consensus. 'We're on the job with my parents?' is a good reveal that escalates the stakes of the central conflict.

jokes.text: Because you're not a monster, all right? Because people don't want to drive what a monster drives.
jokes.setup: Britta asks why liking Avatar is required for selling Hondas
jokes.punchline: Rick's explanation — 'people don't want to drive what a monster drives' — is corporate logic at its most reductive and accidentally revealing: the entire marketing strategy rests on likability, not product quality
jokes.explanation: Sharp line. 'People don't want to drive what a monster drives' is simultaneously a reasonable marketing insight and an absurd reduction of human authenticity to commercial consequence. Rick means it sincerely, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Stop the Honda, Rick! Do you hear me? Use a light press of your foot to engage the highly responsive anti-lock brakes of this incredible vehicle, now!
jokes.setup: Britta is furious and trying to escape the Honda while Rick drives
jokes.punchline: Even in her anger, Britta delivers the Honda's anti-lock brake spec verbatim — she has fully internalized the marketing language without realizing it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. The payoff of Britta being a Level Seven Susceptible despite her anti-corporate convictions arrives here: she's so immersed in the Honda world that her angry outburst is a product commercial. 'Use a light press of your foot to engage the highly responsive anti-lock brakes of this incredible vehicle' delivered in fury is perfect. The character integration is excellent — only Britta would be this oblivious to her own hypocrisy.

jokes.text: When I influence people to buy Honda products... I feel God's pleasure. That's from Chariots of Fire. I love Chariots of Fire. So do I.
jokes.setup: Rick makes a sincere declaration about finding purpose in Honda marketing
jokes.punchline: 'I feel God's pleasure' — a quote from Chariots of Fire about running — is applied to selling cars; both Rick and Britta then confess they love Chariots of Fire, implying they share genuine tastes even inside their marketing relationship
jokes.explanation: Good cultural reference deployed effectively. 'I feel God's pleasure' (Chariots of Fire) applied to car sales is appropriately absurd. The mutual 'I love Chariots of Fire / So do I' is a small tender irony — their one genuine connection is a 1981 running movie.

jokes.text: Also, we have to. Damn it, Britta! Oops.
jokes.setup: Rick and Britta have bonded over Chariots of Fire being a genuine shared interest
jokes.punchline: Rick undercuts the romantic moment — 'Also, we have to' — revealing their Chariots of Fire love is also contractually mandated; Britta's frustrated 'Damn it, Britta!' at herself is funny self-blame; 'Oops' from Rick is a perfect anti-climax
jokes.explanation: Excellent deflation. 'Also, we have to' is a perfect anti-romantic reveal. 'Damn it, Britta!' at herself (blaming herself for her own susceptibility) is a great self-aware beat. 'Oops' from Rick as the button is pitch-perfect — he knows he's blown it. High structure and economy.

jokes.text: Aw, man, you people are everywhere. I was looking for a place to hide. Don't worry. I'm not gonna bother you. Okay, then, give me a gin and tonic.
jokes.setup: Jeff finds Elroy hiding somewhere — apparently both of them went looking for a secluded spot
jokes.punchline: Elroy's 'Don't worry, I'm not gonna bother you' + immediate 'give me a gin and tonic' contradicts his stated intention with the first thing he says
jokes.explanation: Decent beat. The 'not gonna bother you' immediately followed by a drink order is a good quick contradiction. The setup of both Jeff and Elroy coincidentally both hiding is itself funny.

jokes.text: Your friend Jeff booked Natalie is Freezing for the dance. What? Tonight? We got to go! Why aren't you excited? I used to date her. Natalie? Her name is Julie. Why would the band's name be her name? She's an artist.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals he booked Natalie is Freezing; Elroy has a complicated history with the band
jokes.punchline: Jeff makes the same mistake the Dean made — asking if Elroy dated 'Natalie'; Elroy's correction ('Her name is Julie. Why would the band's name be her name? She's an artist.') is a perfect callback mirror of the earlier scene with the Dean
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback structure. The same misunderstanding (assuming the band member is named Natalie) repeated by a different character, with Elroy giving the same indignant explanation that Julie herself gave, is very well-constructed. It deepens the joke while advancing the plot. High structure score.

jokes.text: She messed me up. She messed me up pretty good.
jokes.setup: Elroy reveals a painful romantic history with Julie
jokes.punchline: The doubled-down understatement — 'pretty good' — adds a wry humor to what is clearly deep pain; the economy of two sentences conveying years of damage
jokes.explanation: Economical character revelation. The understatement of 'pretty good' is well-pitched — it's both funny and genuinely melancholy. Sets up the Jeff-Elroy bonding that follows.

jokes.text: Here's to forgetting. Not gonna toast to that.
jokes.setup: Elroy suggests toasting to forgetting his pain
jokes.punchline: Jeff refuses — which is both principled and signals his own relationship with not-forgetting — a small character revelation delivered flat
jokes.explanation: Jeff's refusal is a small but effective character beat. 'Not gonna toast to that' is delivered with the flat moral certainty of someone who knows forgetting is not how you deal. Good economy.

jokes.text: That's the whole problem. Everybody's in such a rush to protect themselves from each other. Sure, yes, you got to defend your castle, but you also got to... What's that thing that castles have? Walls? Come on. A moat? Goes over the moat. Goes over the moat. Enemy knights? Cavalry? Uh, arrows? No. Come on, stop it. Goes like this. Alligators? No! It's one thing. It's mechanical. One mechanical alligator! Are you screwing with me? I don't even know what the hell you're talking about! It's one mechanical thing! It goes over the moat! It goes like this! A catapult! Ow, Jesus! W-What are you doing...
jokes.setup: Jeff makes an extended speech about vulnerability using a castle metaphor
jokes.punchline: He cannot remember 'drawbridge' — the word he's looking for — and the increasingly absurd wrong guesses (alligators, one mechanical alligator, catapult) escalate until someone guesses 'catapult' and apparently punches Jeff
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sustained bits. The escalation of wrong guesses — from 'walls' to 'moat' to 'alligators' to 'ONE MECHANICAL ALLIGATOR' — is perfectly calibrated. 'One mechanical alligator!' is a surreal peak before the whole sequence is ended by an apparent punch. The structure builds expertly: each wrong guess is funnier, Jeff's frustration escalates, and 'catapult' as the final wrong answer ending in physical injury is a great button. High craft, high impact.

jokes.text: A drawbridge. A drawbridge! [long pause, Elroy arrives] You need a drawbridge.
jokes.setup: Earlier, Jeff couldn't remember the word 'drawbridge' in his castle metaphor
jokes.punchline: Several minutes later, Elroy finally produces the word — 'A drawbridge' — delivered with the gravity of a revelation; then again after he walks in, adding 'You need a drawbridge' as both the word and a life lesson
jokes.explanation: The best structured payoff in the episode. The long delay between the setup (the castle escalation sequence) and 'A drawbridge' makes the callback land harder. 'You need a drawbridge' is both the trivial answer Jeff was looking for AND a genuine piece of advice about vulnerability — it means both things simultaneously. The dual function (comedy callback + thematic resonance) is exactly the kind of craft that makes Community exceptional. Near-perfect structure.

jokes.text: It's Elroy's favorite band, too. Really? I once... I once hallucinated one of their music videos in his RV. That's weird.
jokes.setup: Jeff notes the band is at the dance
jokes.punchline: Abed mentions hallucinating the band's music video in Elroy's RV — a bizarre non sequitur delivered as casually as possible — Jeff's 'That's weird' is the underreaction
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — a deeply weird statement delivered with complete normalcy. 'I once hallucinated one of their music videos in his RV' implies a whole story that we don't get, and Abed's nonchalance about hallucinating is perfect. References a prior episode for fans.

jokes.text: No, the Dean can't introduce the band tonight. He's in his office, deciding what kind of vehicles to buy for the athletic department. Yeah, he needs a whole fleet. That's right, a fleet of vehicles. He just needs to pick a model of car. He's in his office. Did you hear that?
jokes.setup: Someone mentions the Dean can't introduce the band
jokes.punchline: Britta and Rick proceed to do an obviously coordinated guerrilla marketing relay — feeding the Dean's susceptibility from a distance through third parties — each one repeating the information with different emphasis, completely transparently
jokes.explanation: Good satire of marketing tactics — the transparent relay of information as a guerrilla marketing technique is funny because it's simultaneously subtle (planting info) and obvious (Britta and Rick are clearly coordinating). Their earnestness about 'we're out of the game, just one more job' is very funny.

jokes.text: Guess I'm a Level Seven Susceptible, too.
jokes.setup: Britta watches Rick go in for one more Honda job despite claiming they were done
jokes.punchline: She identifies herself as a Level Seven Susceptible — susceptible not to advertising but to Rick — the term she coined for the Dean now applies to her own romantic weakness
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The term Britta invented to describe the Dean's advertising weakness is now applied to her own romantic susceptibility — the irony is structural rather than incidental. Britta, the anti-corporate crusader, is the most susceptible person in the episode. Nine words that close the episode's character arc while completing a running gag. High structure, character integration, and economy.

jokes.text: Why do they assume somebody is named Natalie in the band? It, like, happens all the time.
jokes.setup: Julie speaks with someone backstage about the band name confusion
jokes.punchline: 'It happens all the time' — confirming the Natalie confusion is a universal experience for the band, not just a Greendale problem
jokes.explanation: Good running gag extension. 'It happens all the time' is a funny confirmation that the band has fully accepted this as their cross to bear. Closes the Natalie joke thread.

jokes.text: You came after me, because I wasn't interested. You got me interested, and I fell hard. Then, you got bored and destroyed me. And I've been afraid to love anybody for 20 years since, but not anymore.
jokes.setup: Elroy confronts Julie backstage about their history
jokes.punchline: 'But not anymore' — the declaration of emotional breakthrough delivered with Elroy's characteristic understated confidence; the 20-year figure also lands as unexpectedly specific
jokes.explanation: More earnest than comic, but '20 years' is a funny specific that lends dark humor to the scene. The understatement of 'but not anymore' works for the character.

jokes.text: Fine. 'Fine.' That's you. That's my impression of you, you jaded, hipster a-hole.
jokes.setup: Julie responds to Elroy's heartfelt speech with a dismissive 'Fine'
jokes.punchline: Elroy immediately does a one-word impression of her — capturing her entire persona in that single syllable — then labels her 'jaded, hipster a-hole' with the precision of someone who has thought about this for 20 years
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best deliveries. The impression — 'Fine.' — is perfect in its minimalism; it IS a complete impression of a certain type of person. 'You jaded, hipster a-hole' follows with the precision of a diagnosis that's been prepared. Elroy's character is excellently served here: he's funny and right at the same time. High quotability.

jokes.text: I still love your music. Have a great gig.
jokes.setup: Elroy has just called Julie a jaded hipster a-hole
jokes.punchline: He immediately follows up by sincerely complimenting her music and wishing her well — the collision of the insult and the professional courtesy is the joke
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on Elroy's confrontation. 'I still love your music. Have a great gig.' delivered immediately after calling her a hipster a-hole is a great character moment — Elroy is big enough to separate the artist from the person, and he does it with sincere grace and no irony. The sincerity is what makes it funny.

jokes.text: Elroy, I'm tired of playing this game. I like you and I want you to like me. Oh, okay. You're a good guy, Jeff Winger. You and I are gonna be friends. Okay, great. Whatever. I love you.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts Elroy directly about wanting his approval, following the advice to be vulnerable
jokes.punchline: Elroy immediately accepts and says 'I love you' — cutting through Jeff's carefully constructed emotional breakthrough with an easy, warm declaration that Jeff can't quite match ('Okay, great. Whatever.')
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Jeff's arc. Jeff's 'Okay, great. Whatever.' at 'I love you' — reverting to deflection the moment the vulnerability succeeds — is very Jeff. Elroy's immediate warmth vs. Jeff's immediate retreat is a great character contrast. The irony that Jeff worked so hard for this moment and then can't receive it is both funny and true.

jokes.text: Britta, did you know your boyfriend was guerilla marketing for Honda? I knew he represented something I wanted to buy.
jokes.setup: Frankie confirms what everyone knew about Rick
jokes.punchline: Britta's answer — 'I knew he represented something I wanted to buy' — reframes the relationship entirely in marketing terms, acknowledging her susceptibility while also being oddly romantic
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best final character beats. 'I knew he represented something I wanted to buy' works as both a confession (she was susceptible) and as an accidentally beautiful description of falling in love (the person embodies a feeling you want). Britta saying something that is simultaneously self-deprecating, honest, and weirdly poetic is her character at its best. High quotability.

jokes.text: I did good, Frankie. Didn't I do good? Yes. Good Dean. Smart Dean.
jokes.setup: The Dean has apparently been manipulated into buying a fleet of Hondas
jokes.punchline: Frankie's condescending 'Good Dean. Smart Dean.' — praising him like a dog that did a trick — implies everyone knows he was played and he thinks he won
jokes.explanation: Decent beat. Frankie's dog-praising register is funny and appropriate — the Dean is being treated with the exact level of respect this situation deserves. 'Smart Dean' especially lands as sarcasm.

jokes.text: Of course, if you want to come with us... because you are good. I had nothing to do with it. The 2015 Honda CR-V sells itself. That's why it's this year's Motor Trend Sport/Utility of the Year.
jokes.setup: Rick invites Britta to come with him and Honda
jokes.punchline: Britta's self-deprecating 'I had nothing to do with it. The 2015 Honda CR-V sells itself.' — delivered by the character who has been unknowingly selling Honda all episode — is a perfect ironic coda; then 'Motor Trend Sport/Utility of the Year' is the actual Honda product integration credit dropping at the end
jokes.explanation: The episode's most meta joke. Britta delivering the actual Motor Trend award (a real Honda marketing fact) as her character's final line is a layered bit: it's the product placement credit, it's Britta being an unwitting Honda shill one last time, and it acknowledges the entire episode was itself a Honda advertisement. Community's willingness to be this self-aware about branded content is remarkable.

jokes.text: Oh, my. Where did he go? Thank you.
jokes.setup: Rick apparently disappears mysteriously again
jokes.punchline: The Dean's wide-eyed wonder at Rick's disappearing act — followed by 'Thank you' to no one — implies he's genuinely awestruck by Rick's mystique
